request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: The fitted noise is huge (sigma ≈ 45°, rms/sigma = 1.18), so the evidence can only weakly separate models. The free power law (n ≈ 2.05, C ≈ 0.93 GM) still beats Newton by about 15 in ln-evidence. The residuals also carry a clear systematic trend with heliocentric distance: mean east goes from positive to negative, and mean north goes from negative to positive, as r increases. The two half-ellipse fits show a large retrograde apsidal shift (about −44°/orbit) and a period change between halves. These suggest the radial law departs from a pure inverse square. A power law with n > 2 predicts prograde precession, so a retrograde signal points instead to an extra attractive term that grows (relative to Newton) with r. Examples are an added Hooke-like term or a constant inward acceleration. Yukawa is still unfitted and offers a one-parameter alternative that weakens gravity outward. I propose these three single-parameter deformations of Newton, with signed bounds so the data can choose the direction.

proposals.rationale: An extra linear (Hooke-like or distributed-mass) attraction produces retrograde apsidal precession and a distance-dependent deviation, matching the −44°/orbit shift and the r-trend in the residuals.
A constant radial acceleration is the simplest non-inverse-square addition. It also yields retrograde precession and an r-dependent bias, with one parameter.
This registered one-parameter screened-gravity law has not been fitted yet. It tests whether an outward weakening (as the power law with n > 2 suggests) is preferred.
